questions.q: What does it mean that notebook cells are connected to a single running kernel?
options: The kernel only keeps variables alive until the notebook file is saved
Code cells and Markdown cells each get their own independent kernel
Variables defined in one cell stay alive in the kernel's memory and remain available to every other cell, not just the one where they were defined
Each cell runs in a completely separate Python process with no shared memory
questions.explain: A notebook's cells all share one running kernel; once a variable is defined in any executed cell, it persists in that kernel's memory and is visible to subsequently run cells, which is what makes incremental, exploratory work possible.

questions.q: Why is 'Restart Kernel and Run All' described as the real test of whether a notebook is correct?
options: It permanently deletes any cell that previously raised an error
It only runs the Markdown cells, skipping all code cells
It clears all kernel memory and reruns every cell strictly in page order, exposing any hidden dependency on cells having been run out of their visual order
It automatically fixes any bugs in the code before running it
questions.explain: Because execution order in the kernel isn't necessarily page order, a notebook can appear to work during exploratory out-of-order runs but fail once run strictly top-to-bottom from a clean kernel -- which is exactly what Restart Kernel and Run All tests.

questions.q: What does the execution count shown as `In [3]:` next to a code cell actually indicate?
options: That the cell is the third cell from the top of the notebook
That the cell has been edited 3 times since the notebook was created
That the cell took 3 seconds to run
That the cell was the third one executed in the current kernel session, regardless of where it physically sits on the page
questions.explain: The execution count records which numbered run in the kernel session produced that cell's current output -- it tracks actual run order, which can differ from the cell's visual position on the page.

questions.q: Why does the lesson avoid printing a specific invented timing result for `%timeit`?
options: Because the exact numbers %timeit reports depend on the specific machine and current system load, so a fixed printed number wouldn't be a real, verifiable result
Because %timeit cannot be used to compare NumPy against plain Python loops
Because %timeit only works on Markdown cells, not code cells
Because %timeit is deprecated and no longer works in modern Jupyter
questions.explain: Timing results are hardware- and load-dependent, so the lesson explicitly avoids inventing a fixed number and instead tells you to run %timeit yourself to see the real result on your own machine.

questions.q: Why can't a `.ipynb` file simply be run with `python notebook.ipynb`, and what is `jupyter nbconvert --to script` used for?
options: A `.ipynb` file can already be run directly with the python command exactly like a `.py` script

A `.ipynb` file stores cells, outputs, and metadata as JSON rather than plain Python; `nbconvert --to script` extracts the code into a plain `.py` file that can be run directly, which also helps check it doesn't depend on out-of-order execution
nbconvert is only used to delete a notebook's saved outputs, with no connection to exporting to a script
`.ipynb` files are actually plain Python files with a different file extension, so `nbconvert` is purely cosmetic
questions.explain: A notebook file is JSON containing cells/outputs/metadata, not a runnable script on its own. Converting to a plain .py file via nbconvert makes it runnable top-to-bottom, which doubles as a check for hidden out-of-order dependencies.
